messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 80
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Social Worker
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
  pcl5: 66

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Male Presence: Being alone with men, Known People: Related people, Auditory (Door): Doors opening or slamming
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Memory Erasure: I try to erase the memory of the event, Meaning Seeking: I think about why the event has happened to me
  Threat: Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Scanning Exits: I scan for exits as soon as I enter any room or building, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Confused Sequence: I cannot put the memories of the event in the right order, Snapshot Memory: I remember the frightening event as a few moments, and each moment is a picture in my mind., Grief on Recall: When I remember the event I feel overwhelming grief
  Negative Appraisals: Shattered Beliefs: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed, Contamination: I feel dirty or contaminated because of what happened, Mistrust: People can't be trusted

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

At eighty years old, Eleanor Vance had believed she understood the architecture of a good life, one built on a foundation of predictable kindness and mutual respect. A long career as a social worker had fortified this belief; she had seen the worst of things, but always held that systems, and people, could ultimately be trusted. Meeting Arthur two years ago had felt like a capstone to that life, a partnership for her final decades. That foundation crumbled six months ago, on a Tuesday afternoon. The memory doesn’t play like a film for her. Instead, it is a series of stark, silent photographs burned into her mind: the heavy oak of their apartment door slamming shut with a deafening crack, the contorted anger on Arthur’s face under the hallway light, the pattern of the floral wallpaper in the corner she was backed into. She cannot string these moments together into a coherent sequence, but the images float up, untethered from time, bringing with them a wave of grief so profound it feels like drowning.

In the weeks that followed, Eleanor’s world began to shrink. The first thing to go was sleep. She would lie awake for hours, heart pounding, listening to the old building settle, certain that every creak was a footstep. She started staying up until two or three in the morning, reading in her armchair until sheer exhaustion took over, a desperate strategy to avoid the nightmares that waited for her in the dark. During the day, a relentless watchfulness took hold. When her nephew, Mark, came to visit, she couldn't relax. She found herself tracking his every move, her body tensed for a threat she couldn't name but felt in her bones. The sound of the elevator door opening on her floor would send a jolt of adrenaline through her. After she cancelled their weekly dinner for the third time, Mark stopped asking. She felt the loss of his company keenly, but the thought of being alone with any man, even one she had helped raise, was simply unbearable.

Her professional instincts turned inward, twisting into a painful, circular logic. She spends hours trying to understand *why* it happened, replaying conversations, searching for a missed sign, a misstep on her part that could have prevented it. This quest for meaning provides no answers, only a deepening conviction that the world she knew was a fiction. Her core belief system, once a source of strength, has been completely destroyed. People, she has come to believe, cannot be trusted. Safety is an illusion. This new reality dictates her every action. Before entering the local library or the grocery store, she pauses on the threshold, her eyes darting from one exit to another, mapping escape routes before she dares to step inside.

Eleanor feels a profound sense of being soiled, contaminated by the event. She showers twice a day, scrubbing her skin raw, but the feeling of being unclean lingers. She tries to consciously push the memory away, to will the photographic snapshots out of her mind, but they always return, vivid and sharp. It was the growing isolation that finally prompted her to seek help. The silence in her apartment had become as loud as the slamming door in her memory. She is terrified that she is permanently broken, that the trust and openness that defined her for eight decades are gone for good. More than anything, she hopes to one day feel safe in her own home again, to be able to hear a door close without her body preparing for an attack that is already over.
